title: Malibu’s Bryson Fire Containment Grows To 39% As Wind Conditions Begin To Improve
full_text: Skip to main content By Tom Tapp , Patrick Hipes October 16, 2026 6:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source A firefighting helicopter flies over the Bryson Fire in Malibu Justin Sullivan/Getty Images UPDATED with latest: Improving wind conditions helped firefighters make progress on the Bryson Fire north of Malibu on Friday, with the latest reports saying the brushfire is now 39% contained. The fire has consumed an estimated 147 acres as of a report this afternoon by the Los Angeles County Fire Department, which has had jurisdiction over the brushfire since first responding at about 4:40 p.m. Thursday near the intersection of Mulholland Highway and Encinal Canyon Road. According to Cal Fire, a total of 414 personnel and two helicopters have been battling the blaze, which is centralized north of Encinal between the former Malibu Golf Club and Saddlerock Ranch. TV reports Thursday night had the blaze starting next to the Camp Kilpatrick juvenile detention center. Two zones in the area are under mandatory evacuation, though none in the city of Malibu; evacuation warnings are still in place in western Malibu. Road closures include Decker Road and Encinal Canyon Road, Kanan Road and Mulholland Highway, and Mulholland and Westlake Boulevard. PCH remains open. Watch on Deadline Courtesy of Cal Fire The National Weather Service has red-flag warnings in effect for much of Los Angeles and southeastern Ventura counties until 8 p.m. Saturday, with reports of wind gusts in the local mountains reaching 50-70 mph Friday. The NWS expects that the Santa Ana wind event, which coupled with high temperatures and low humidity causes the dangerous conditions, to subside this evening. The NWS said today that it expects the winds to be 10-15 mph weaker Saturday. PREVIOUSLY, Friday, 12:30 AM: A wind-whipped brushfire ignited in western Malibu Thursday and spread from one to five acres in a matter of about 15 minutes. Within an hour, the incident was estimated at about 35 acres, including various spot fires that erupted as winds pushed the flames forward. As of 11:30 p.m., the fire was estimated at more than 146 acres with 5% containment and moving SSW. The National Weather Service has forecast the winds “to increase significantly overnight, [with] gusts of 50 to 60 mph possible.” Dubbed the Bryson Fire, the blaze was first reported shortly before 5 p.m. near the intersection of Mulholland Highway and Encinal Canyon Road. The ignition point seems to be just north of Encinal in between the former Malibu Golf Club and Saddlerock Ranch. More specifically, TV reports have the blaze starting right next to the Camp Kilpatrick juvenile detention center. The Bryson Fire is now more than 100 acres. Very close to the Malibu Golf Club. Firefighters trying to keep it from jumping Mulholland pic.twitter.com/O3eJOQ8h7b — Matthew Seedorff (@MattSeedorff) October 16, 2026 According to the Watch Duty app, an Evacuation Order was issued for the south of the fire in Zuma and Trancas Canyons, where the wind is pushing the blaze. It was later extended west of the area where the event began. The Los Angeles County Probation Department announced that it safely evacuated 38 youths from Camp Kilpatrick. Evacuation Warnings were issued from the L.A. County line in the north and south toward Point Dume. An Evacuation Order means “leave now,” while an Evacuation Warning means “be ready to leave.” See the Order area in red and Warning in orange below (as of 7:30 p..m.). The road closures in the area include Decker Road, Encinal Canyon Road, Kanan Road, Mulholland Highway and Westlake Boulevard. Fire officials were most concerned with keeping the blaze north of Encinal Canyon Road, one of the few natural firebreaks in the immediate area. The concern is, should it jump Encinal Canyon Road, the flames could get pushed directly down Zuma, Trancas and other canyons on a run to the Coast. By 10:30 p.m., the fire’s perimeter on its southwest flank had spread right down to Encinal. See perimeter map below. The much larger Woolsey fire made a similar run in 2018 after starting in Chatsworth and burning around and through portions of Calabasas and Agoura Hills when, according to an account in the Malibu Times, “It burned through multiple canyons simultaneously, driven at first by 60 mph Santa Ana winds, and then by the wind generated by the heat of fire itself” all the way down to Point Dume. Footage from KTLA of a firefighting helicopter dropping water on the huge flames of the #BrysonFire north of Malibu, California. In 2 hours it has burned 101.5 acres and continues to spread, prompting evacuations. #CAwx pic.twitter.com/gUuUPkJzGD — Collin Gross (@CollinGrossWx) October 16, 2026 Santa Ana winds were fanning the fire out of the NE at about 19 mph with gusts to 36 in the early evening, according to a National Weather Service reading for the Malibu Hills. At 7:30 p.m., the temperature was 80 degrees with a relative humidity of 14%. The area is sparsely populated with private estates set atop hills or within canyons, making firefighting access difficult. Among the properties in the area are Saddlerock Ranch, a location used in filming The Kardashians , The Bachelor, The Bachelorette, The Biggest Loser, Better Things, Knight Rider and The A-Team . Also nearby is the historic Calamigos Ranch , home to shoots for Grey’s Anatomy , Love Is Blind, The Bachelorette , The Bachelor, Beverly Hills 90210, Rizzoli & Isles , The Biggest Loser and Wayne’s World 2 . The last major blaze to sweep through the area was the 2018 Woolsey Fire, meaning brush in most of those canyons has not been cleared for about eight years. Water-dropping helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft were dispatched to the scene. A first-alarm response had also been requested from Ventura County FD. With night set to fall, many in the area were without power due to outages planned by Southern California Edison in hopes of preventing power lines downed by the winds from sparking fires. See hashmarked areas on the map below for those outages. The good news is that the winds are expected to lay down after dark. The bad news is that, if the fire persists, the worst of this Santa Ana wind event is still expected Friday morning. title: Angie Nixon Says Black Republican Byron Donalds “Doesn’t Support Black People”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All October 16, 2026 5:37pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon speaks during a campaign event at the St. John Missionary Baptist Church on September 28, 2026 in Boynton Beach, Florida. Nixon faces incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody (R-FL) in the November 3rd general election, one of several Florida races that are heating up Joe Raedle/Getty Images Florida is becoming one of the bigger enigmas of the already-puzzling 2026 election season. Democrats are showing themselves to be surprisingly competitive. Democrat David Jolly is running neck-and-neck with Trump-approved Republican Byron Donalds in two of three recent polls for the governor job. And Jacksonville legislator and DSA member Angie Nixon , having upset moderate Democrat Alex Vindman in the primary, now is at least keeping it close against Republican incumbent Ashley Moody. All of which is startling in a state that went for Donald Trump by 13 points just two years ago and hasn’t elected a Democratic governor since 1994. Related Stories News Half a Scaramucci: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Ousted After One Briefing Business BBC Asks Judge to Force Trump to Sit for Deposition in His Own Lawsuit Against Broadcaster Now Nixon is turning up the heat on Republican candidates. On an upcoming episode of Crooked Media’s YouTube show Long Play, Nixon lets it fly against the Republican gubernatorial candidate. “Byron Donalds doesn’t support Black people,” she tells hosts Jennifer Palmieri and Errin Haines on camera in an early cut of the episode, which debuts Monday. Haines then follows up by asking Nixon to explain what she means when she says that Donalds is “going to bring back the worst parts of our history.” Nixon replies, “I mean, he is someone who said that Black people were better off during the Jim Crow era.” The race has grown contentious but seems to be reaching a new level of fervor as it heads into the final two weeks. Nixon has said at rallies that she wants to keep funding the police, referring to a common anti-DSA knock, because she wants Moody, Ron DeSantis and Trump locked up. For his part, vice president J.D. Vance said recently at a rally, addressing Nixon, “Get the hell out of here, you don’t belong in America.” (Nixon in the episode: “They don’t have anything to run on but cruelty.”) Meanwhile, Donalds has been criticized by Jolly for not extending leniency to young people that he was shown when he was arrested on drug charges as a young man and given the opportunity of a diversion program; a hot-button new ad has a retired U.S. General calling Donalds “weak” and a “hypocrite” for it. (Palmieri and Haines discuss the ad in the new episode.) Launched earlier this year , Long Play examines the divisions and shifting political alignments in various Southern states. After concluding its first season with trips to Georgia, Texas and other Southern states, the show kicks off its second season ahead of the midterms with a Florida episode. Five flagship and three bonus episodes are planned, straddling both sides of the midterms and set in Texas and Georgia, where close Senate races are unfolding, among other states. The overall goal remains to recalibrate perceptions of the region as a GOP stronghold, which principals say is far too simplistic and out of date. In Florida, Donalds has looked to court the Black vote to gain the governorship. “You’ve been faithful to that [Democratic] party, have they been faithful to you?,” he recently told an audience at HBCU Florida A&M. Donalds would be Florida’s first Black governor, though has struggled to gain support of large numbers of Black voters, even losing 17 counties in August’s primary to white opponents. As for the Senate, flipping a Florida seat blue (the seat Nixon is seeking is currently held by Moody, who was appointed two years ago when Marco Rubio was named Secretary of State), is a nice-to-have for Florida Democrats but not seen as essential in retaking control of the Senate. Nixon says on the show that she thinks a win for her is viable. “So, honestly, there’s a whole bunch of polls,” says Nixon, as she seeks to become both the first Black senator and first female Democratic Senator in Florida’s history. “There are some ranging from tied to seven points. Recently, one was two, I was two points down, like, yesterday. And so the only poll that matters is the Election Day poll.” In an email, Palmieri said that “My takeaway is neither party can ever write off Florida. It’s too big, too dynamic to take for granted…any outcome is possible.” Added Haines: “The 2026 midterm cycle has been unpredictable — and Florida is arguably one of the biggest examples of that unpredictability.” Palmieri, a former Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama comms exec who also cohosted Showtime staple The Circus , and Haines, editor-at-large for The 19th, co-host the show with contributions from former NOLA mayor Mitch Landrieu. Circus producer Left/Right produces, and Crooked Media fixture Jon Favreau exec produces. A companion podcast will also be released. THR

title: The Impossible ‘Whalefall’: Director Brian Duffield Wanted a Challenge, So He Discovered a Way to Crush Austin Abrams in a Whale Stomach That Left Onlookers ‘Baffled’
full_text: Dan Doperalski for Variety Turns out that it’s tough to shoot in a whale’s stomach. “ Whalefall ” director Brian Duffield is gleefully outlining some of the biggest hurdles while shooting his new movie. The premise for the film, in theaters now via 20th Century Studios, is simple: A young diver named Jay ( Austin Abrams ) is accidentally swallowed by a whale, ends up in its stomach and must escape before his tank of oxygen runs out. It’s a lean idea, but required an innovative and energetic leader like Duffield to get the claustrophobic shots done on practical sets. Related Stories Danielle Ponder Meshes Old-School Soul With Future Sounds on the Dazzling ‘Everything Has Changed’: Album Review 'Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald' Review: Judd Apatow's Juicy and Haunting Portrait of a Comedy Star as Troubled as He Was Hilarious “It’s such a small space and essentially a 360-degree set,” he says. “There’s a couple portals you can kind of shove a camera through, but it’s also somewhat full of water. All the lighting of the coil is inside the set. Basically everything that you would have on a normal movie set, we’re putting inside of a very small space. It’s also on a gimbal that’s rocking and rolling. So you take your normal film set footprint and then you put it into a bag. And then you also put Austin Abrams into the bag, and then sometimes other animals. If Austin’s wrong an inch, it doesn’t really work. Everyone’s cramped in this little doorway. But he can’t hear us, because the rubber is so thick inside.” Popular on Variety Duffield smiles at the outrageous setup. “I was talking to a director,” he says. “He had a question and I sent him pictures of the set. And he was just like, ‘You’ve got to be joking.’ From when the whale is chewing Austin, it’s just a bunch of big, burly men jumping on the set and crushing down on him. And he’s in there, screaming and drowning with a real oxygen tank. I’m looking at this little monitor and if he needs help, it’s going to sound the exact same. Every time you call cut, you’re just hoping that the screaming stops. We had the studio come to set and watch this thing. From the outside it just looked so silly. I remember Disney safety reps would come and just be watching it, saying, ‘I genuinely don’t know if this is safe.’ But we worked hard, really hard to make sure Austin was safe.” Brian Duffield photographed at the PMC Studio in Los Angeles. Dan Doperalski for Variety Everyone made it out of the shoot unharmed, but the finished product is filled with harrowing set-pieces that are sure to push audiences to the brink. Duffield understood the vision early on, as he reached out to novelist Daniel Kraus on social media when he first heard the premise of the novel of the same name, before it was even published. He read an advance copy of the 2023 book, and was quickly swept away with the cinematic promise it held. Duffield ended up co-writing the “Whalefall” script with Kraus. “You get the initial ‘boy inside a whale’ story, which definitely tickled all the genre parts of my brain,” Duffield says. “The idea of making a movie that had never been made before is always really appealing to me. It’s instantly clear how challenging that was, and I was really looking for a challenge. I was hungry to just keep pushing myself and the crew that I had consistently been working with. I think we just had the appetite at the time to take a big swing.” Duffield is no stranger to ambitious projects. He began his Hollywood career as a writer with a disparate group of scripts, including a big-budget sequel (2015’s “The Divergent Series: Insurgent”), a Western (2015’s “Jane Got a Gun”), a slasher (2017’s “The Babysitter”) and a sci-fi action movie (2020’s “Underwater”). He transitioned into an idiosyncratic directing career with 2020’s “Spontaneous” (logline: a romance is shaded by the fact that people start spontaneously combusting) and 2023’s “No One Will Save You,” a nearly dialogue-free alien invasion movie. Beyond their high concepts, Duffield’s works are marked by an emotional heft, which is no different in “Whalefall.” Jay’s diving trip is prompted by him trying to locate the body of his estranged father Mitt (Josh Brolin) after he dies by suicide. He’d never be able make amends with, or come to an understanding with his father, a theme that resonates through much of the story. “I don’t think I was looking for a father-son story, but I think I needed a father-son story,” Duffield, a parent himself, says. “As soon as I was reading it, I couldn’t stop thinking about … not the whale, but about Jay and Mitt in that relationship. I thought, ‘That was the magic trick of the book.’ You’re forgetting about squids and acid and you’re thinking more about how these two guys are thinking they want nothing more than to spend time together, but they can’t quite express how they need to spend time in a different way.” Brian Duffield photographed at the PMC Studio in Los Angeles in October 2026. Dan Doperalski for Variety While Abrams and Brolin were able to bring the emotional gravitas to flashback scenes chronicling key moments in their frayed relationship, shooting the in-whale scenes was the overarching creative challenge. “I had plenty of directors come and visit and all of them just looked so baffled,” Duffield says. “I had general confusion about how we were doing what we were doing. The thing I’ve learned the most is the joy of making movies for me is the crew and getting to hire a lot of the same people over and over again. I think if I have any gift as a director, it’s hiring people that are extremely talented, Oscar winners and whatnot. I like spending time with them and feel comfortable asking advice. I trust them if I feel like they have a note or an idea — it’s probably good.” It’s part of a larger ethos Duffield brings to every project. “I want to feel the effort, and I want to feel like I’m becoming a better filmmaker because of it,” he says. title: How ‘Whalefall’s Director & Author Wove The Closure Of A Father-Son Relationship Into A Survival Tale
full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi How ‘Whalefall’s Director & Author Wove The Closure Of A Father-Son Relationship Into A Survival Tale The Smashing Pumpkins Release Latest ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Album Track, ‘Black Stars’ Everything We Know About ‘The Housemaid’s Secret’ Film So Far View All October 16, 2026 4:20pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Director Brian Duffield and Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner in 20th Century Studios' WHALEFALL Jennifer Clasen/20th Century Studios SPOILER ALERT: This story spoils the plot of the film Whalefall , now out in theaters, based on Daniel Kraus ‘ novel. A running joke Whalefall director Brian Duffield had going to summarize the film hailing from 20 th Century Studios and Imagine Entertainment and hitting theaters this week was that “men would rather get swallowed by a sperm whale than go to therapy.” Just as Austin Abrams ’ Jay Gardiner finds himself in quite the harrowing predicament trapped in a whale’s stomach after a tangle with a squid, the cast, crew and filmmakers of Whalefall also found themselves in the tricky situation of bringing the premise of Daniel Kraus’ novel to the big screen. Related Stories Reviews ‘Whalefall’ Review: Austin Abrams Wrestles With Grief, Toxic Masculinity & Grotesque Whale Innards In Emotionally Gutsy Body Horror News 20th Century’s ‘Whalefall’ Producers Reflect On Shooting In California: “The Best Creative Teams Are Here” To back up, Jay’s decision to seek out the remains of his dead father Mitt Gardiner ( Josh Brolin ), who has committed suicide by drowning in the Pacific Ocean following a diagnosis of mesothelioma, is what really landed him in this situation. Just as he has to get scrappy and use anything he can find to escape, those behind the making of the movie had to be in constant communication about what it would take to pull off such intense scenes, many of which took place inside a life-sized whale stomach built specifically for the film. Watch on Deadline “It takes a village to build a whale, and I think it takes a really great village to survive it. And that’s been really one of the most gratifying parts of [production],” Duffield said when Deadline visited the set of the movie at Radford Studios in L.A. in September, during an early tank scene where Abrams encountered the whale for the first time. “It’s such a new and unique challenge that I think we hired the right people, because it was a lot of us all banging our heads together trying to figure out how to shoot every day.” Multiple whale stomach models were built by Weta Workshop in New Zealand, with the head, throat, esophagus and larynx constructed in California because they were too big to ship to set on time. The 12-foot-tall, 18-foot-long whale head was manufactured by StudioArt & Technology. Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner in 20th Century Studios’ ‘Whalefall’ 20th Century Studios “It’s such an interlocked set. I’ve never made a movie, and I can’t imagine ever making a movie where every single department really has to be talking to each other every step of the way,” Duffield said. “For the stomach, Ramsey [Avery] our production designer [had] to figure out how to build it, and then we [had] to figure out how to put cameras in it, but then also we had to figure out how to light it, and then the lights become bioluminescence. Visual effects supervisor Guillaume Rocheron, who worked on Jordan Peele’s Nope , rigged the LED lighting in the stomach to eventually render as the bioluminescence that then helps illuminate Jay’s environment. “Some colors do not show up the same color in LED lights. So, our costume designer had to build Austin’s costume around what the LEDs would show up with,” Duffield added. “So we would take neoprene samples to New Zealand, where we built the stomachs, to show them under the lights, against the whale skin, to see what colors show up.” Cameras and lenses were broken “nonstop” during filming; the crew ultimately constructed scenes around the one spot the camera could actually fit into the cramped space and worked backwards from that vantage point. If that weren’t claustrophobic enough, Abrams also faced the added challenge of emoting behind a facemask and the diving equipment Jay uses. “We redesigned the regulator to make it as small as possible, because regulators are not really meant to be worn outside of water. And yet, the air inside the whale stomach is toxic. It won’t kill him, necessarily, but it’s full of methane and things that make him a little high,” Duffield said. “So we redesigned the regulator to give him as much mouth shape as possible. He actually does talk throughout the movie to himself or to other characters in the stomach. That has been a challenging learning curve.” Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner 20th Century Studios These formidable aspects of the film’s creation echoe Kraus’ general approach to writing books; he now has 30-plus under his belt. “I like to create new problems and have to fight through the solutions — I try to start with an impossible [conceit] where I just throw hurdles in front of me of things that I don’t know,” Kraus told Deadline on set. “So I have to relearn how to write a book every time.” The impetus for Whalefall came from a viral video in which a kayaker ended up in the mouth of a whale. Once Kraus heard about the clip, it spawned discussions with friends about whether it could actually happen. He could not stop thinking about it. Following an email to author friend Mary Roach, author of Gulp: Adventures on the Alimentary Canal (2013), and correspondence with three whale experts she recommended, Kraus had found the “high concept” hook for the book, which hit shelves in 2023. “I didn’t want to do it if it couldn’t really happen — being swallowed by a whale has been treated like a fable and Biblical stories forever. My interest was, could you do it scientifically accurately?” Kraus said. “And by the end of the day, I was all systems go. All the whale experts were super-excited to help, and they think about whales all day, but never in this context. We were off to the races.” Both Duffield and Kraus drew connections to the science fiction genre in different ways, with Kraus developing an interest in whales during the frontloaded research process for the book, which took about three months. “I became more and more … obsessed, you might say, with whales,” he said. “There’s a lot of what I was doing with this biology of a whale, but I also unexpectedly started to get really enamored of whales as a being, as a force of nature. “Sperm whales are extraordinarily intelligent. They’re one of the most mysterious animals on the planet. Everything about them is strange. They really feel like aliens. Even in the deep ocean, which is filled with alien-like creatures, the whales almost feel like a master alien. They’re not aggressors. They’re very peaceful animals. Sperm whales have been witnessed helping humans many, many times, like divers in trouble.” Experiencing a whale from the inside out adds complicated layers to Whalefall ‘s story, even when it comes to the father-son relationship at its heart. “How do you fall in love with a character through its guts, basically? It’s definitely gross, but what are the ways that we can fall in love with this animal, because Austin is in such a unique situation, and I think there’s something interesting about his character, who is very fond of of animals and nature,” Duffield said. “One of the things that differentiates his character and Josh’s character is Josh is very hard and Austin’s very soft. But they both have this love of nature, and so giving Austin moments that he can really, for lack of a better way to put it, appreciate how cool the situation is — while also being scared sh*tless and thinking he’s going to die pretty much at any given moment — that was part of the craft of it, too.” Duffield evidently shared a similar awe. For him, the trick with the stomach being the setting for a majority of the movie was balancing the claustrophobic feeling of Jay’s plight with breaks from the cramped space. “It’s challenging for a couple reasons. One, it’s such a long stretch of the movie, and quite a lot happens while he’s in in the stomach, but it was also about keeping it fresh and interesting so [that] after 30 minutes, people weren’t just like, ‘Alright, I’m sick of this stomach,’” Duffield said. “[Jay] does have different little side adventures. He spends some time in the second stomach, which is very visually different, and then in the esophagus of the whale as well. Different animals that are also in the stomachs, and different problems he has to MacGyver his way out of, so it’s just trying to figure out how to keep it fresh visually, which Daniel honestly just did a lot of in the book.” Whalefall executive prodcuer Doug Merrifield, whose credits include the Free Willy films, joined Duffield, Kraus and Imagine Entertainment’s Allen Mandelbaum in emphasizing that the whale is not the villain in the movie. It’s orcas that attack Jay’s sperm whale that ultimately provide the antagonists and the catalyst for the film’s climax. “The whale is not a bad guy. The whale is just an animal that’s doing what it’s meant to be doing. The whale is not interested in [Jay]. It’s trying to get a squid, and Austin is in the way,” Duffield said. “The movie makes a very direct correlation, eventually, between Josh Brolin and and the whale, and part of Austin’s journey is making peace with his dad, who is dead at the start of the movie.” L-R: Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner and Josh Brolin as Mitt Gardiner 20th Century Studios One of the main threads of the book that drew Duffield to directing the adaptation was the father-son relationship at its core; his own son was 4 at the time of the set visit. In Whalefall , Mitt and Jay didn’t always know how best to communicate with each other; the ocean is where they find common ground. “The miracle of the book and hopefully of the movie is, when it ends, you primarily are talking about the relationships, and then the whale is third or fourth build, which for a movie that’s set almost entirely inside of a whale feels impossible, but somehow [Kraus] pulls it off,” Duffield said. “As you age up, you start viewing things from different perspectives. I think before I was a dad, I probably would have been firmly in Jay’s point of view, and then now being on the other side of it and having a son — granted, my son just turned 4, so it’s a very different than the relationship between [Jay] and [Mitt] — [I’m] really starting to feel for Brolin’s character, and understand him to some extent.” Kraus, who grew up in conservative small-town Iowa, leaned into the personal when it came to building the tension of Mitt and Jay’s relationship. His father was a hunter, not as extreme as Mitt, but still an inspiration for the character. “I’m a product of [where I grew up], which is to say, I have avoided getting therapy. I’m a product of that culture where you don’t express yourself and you don’t show your feelings when it comes to interpersonal things,” Kraus said. “Mitt is a very emotional guy when it comes to the ocean, like he will fight tooth and nail for every living creature in there. He’ll do whatever it takes to protect the ocean. But when it comes to dealing with his son, he’s absolutely clueless. He would be much better at interacting with a whale than he would be his son. And ultimately, Mitt becomes the whale, in a sense, and through the whale, they are able to have the conversation.” As Jay fights nitrogen narcosis — a condition in divers in which certain gases take on an anesthetic effect in the nervous system, resulting in a kind of high — and the methane in the whale’s stomach, he has flashbacks that help him piece together info he needs for his survival. The memories often involve his father imparting pearls of wisdom, regardless of whether Jay though of them that way at the time. “The challenge really was, the book has probably 50 flashbacks where it’s constantly hopping back and forth. In the movie, [we had] to take all that information that Jay needs to know scattered across all those flashbacks, and find ways to pack them into vastly fewer flashbacks,” Kraus said. “That was really the biggest challenge.” A small creative detail further merges Mitt and the whale, who speak as one character in Kraus’ book. “The whale’s heart is beating, and the stomach is reacting to the beats of the whale’s heart. So that’s sound puppeteering the stomach. There’s water in it, which is moving from that. And then, on top of all of that, just to show how full circle it starts to go, the whale’s heart is Josh Brolin’s heartbeat,” explained Duffield, who came up with the idea. “We’ve recorded Josh’s heartbeat, and then our sound guys made it a whale heartbeat that is playing.” L-R: Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner and Josh Brolin as Mitt Gardiner 20th Century Studios This detail also fits in with Kraus’ thematic vision. “When I came across the concept of a whalefall, which is when a whale dies and its corpse sinks to the bottom of the ocean, and its body, as it decomposes, sets off a shock wave of life, generations of life are born from its remains,” Kraus said. “ I found that very emotional and touching to the idea that when a whale dies, or somebody we know and love dies, that their death sort of begets life, the memory of them, the influence of them. It goes on, and it goes on for generations, and even when I talk about it now, I get goosebumps, it’s just such a beautiful thought.” Sometimes it takes getting stuck inside a whale to provide some perspective. ‘Street Fighter’ Socking Away $30M; A24’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc Eyes $12M J.K. title: How ‘You Can See Everything’ Exacts Hollywood’s Revenge on Big Tech
full_text: × Skip to main content Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder speak onstage at the 'You Can See Everything' premiere during the 64th New York Film Festival at Alice Tully Hall, Lincoln Center on Sept. 30, 2026 in New York. Cindy Ord/Getty Images for FLC [No spoilers! ] Life may be too short for long-term grudges, as the quote goes, but it’s still lengthy enough to dole out some justice. This weekend, A24 brings out Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything , the Elizabeth Holmes doc that is already creating a major stir with filmgoers after previously dazzling critics. The opening follows the releases last weekend of Mus k , The Social Reckoning and the New York Film Festival premiere of Artificial . All four films contend with the tech alphas trying to remake our lives in their image. And they exact a kind of revenge at once inevitable and improbable. You know the alpha types — those talkers on CNBC or in your college WhatsApp group saying there’s a solution for everything, even to things you didn’t know were problems. Actually, they don’t say there’s a solution — they say there’s a solve, w hich should tip you off right there. Never get involved in a land war in Asia, and never trust anyone who seamlessly turns a verb into a noun. He’s probably trying to sell you something from behind his puffer jacket. Far from the usual stake-less Hollywood gaze, these docs and fact-based dramas center three figures deeply relevant to our current landscape: Elon Musk , Mark Zuckerberg and Sam Altman . (Add any more of them and we might think it’s a Donald Trump state dinner.) The fourth figure, You Can See Everything ’s Holmes along with her husband Billy Evans, is less relevant, but the pair embody a Silicon Valley attitude that survives and dominates even as one half of it sits in a Texas prison: that with a little pluck and a lot of smooth talk anything can be achieved, reality be damned. But it’s not just filmmakers’ decision to center these figures that matters: it’s how they take them on. Musk s pends four hours meticulously deconstructing the ways its subject got his power and the surveillance and even alleged potential-election rigging he is using it for. Reckoning shows a Meta intent on stoking our rage and divisions for its own profiteering. Artificial , which arrives in theaters on Christmas, may be the most searing of the lot. Ostensibly a procedural account of Sam Altman’s rise to power at OpenAI, Luca Guadagnino’s drama (complete with an Oscar-level performance from Andrew Garfield) brutally takes apart how Altman hustled investors and even his own staff — including the engineering prodigy Ilya Sutskever. Sutskever joined and made possible OpenAI’s breakthrough science after Altman reassured him everything would be done all human-centric and responsible. Whoops. Audiences may justifiably seethe at how Sutskever’s safety-first mindset gets steamrolled by Altman’s slick accelerationism (as happened in real life). But we also might want to take heart in how the very fact that we’re watching this account represents its own kind of triumph, as the safety concerns Sutskever worried would be silenced are being megaphoned into the very theater in which our rage curdles. Winning the P.R. war isn’t the same as winning the Wall Street one, of course. But it doesn’t stand apart from it either — not least because companies need some pretty heavy consumer adoption to pull off their financial coup. Even as Musk rolled out to theaters nationwide, homepages told of how Musk’s SpaceX appeared to manipulate Starshield such that it limited Ukraine’s ability to ward off Russian attacks, the man becoming in real-time the policy oligarch Gibney’s film intimates. In all these movies you can’t help sensing a kind of authorial revenge. Aaron Sorkin, sitting down to tell us how mad he is at what Zuckerberg has done in the 15 years since he last visited with him, with not much Zuckerberg can do to respond. Or Gibney, by his own telling, shines a light on the power Musk is gaining over all our lives, with little recourse but to lash out scatologically on the social platform he owns. (X, TikTok, Meta and YouTube all at first denied ads for the film; the latter two, at least, came to their senses.) Altman, meanwhile, was left to simper that “I don’t think they’re going for accuracy,” which he did to Vanity Fair on the day of the Artificial premiere, clearly worried that accurate is exactly how we’ll perceive it. In all of this we have a collection of great dramas — if you haven’t booked your ticket to hoot and gasp at YCSE , go do so now — but also the latest turn in a greater meta-drama, lowercase m, between artists and Silicon Valley, a bow-shot from human storytellers to the masters and sellers of computer code. Tech leaders thought that the magic of LLMs had rid us of all that professional wordsmithing for good. These writers and creators come to say not so fast. After all these years of hearing about (and sometimes already living the idea of) AI coming for Hollywood jobs, some of the people who work at them finally get to say their piece, with everyone listening. This sudden storyteller leverage is literalized by, well, Fielder’s face, which, to every Holmes or Evans desperate fib, subtly contorts into skepticism or disbelief, giving that not only does he know he is being fed con-ish hooey, but also that he and co-director Lance Oppenheim have the power to cast it as such the minute they enter the edit room. What’s more, Holmes and Evans seem to know it too. At one point Evans stomps in to a Fielder secondary interview to try to stop it. You could almost smell the algorithmic impotency in the face of human vitality. In that moment vibrates the larger, call it…trans-cinematic message of the four films — “Engineers may live in our screens and even addict our brains, but the storytellers have something even more powerful: they can make us feel.” The people shaping these four narratives are all singing the same chorus — that much of what they do (and human thought generally) can’t be outsourced to a machine. “I’m not particularly charismatic or good-looking,” Artificial screenwriter Simon Rich told the NYFF audience, “but as a last-ditch effort to warn mankind I wrote this movie.” (Lisa Kudrow and Michael Patrick King’s latest season of The Come back also boldly trafficked in this Hollywood vs the Machines theme.) Perhaps the most surprising part of this filmmaker uprising is that it’s also turned Hollywood studios into something they haven’t been in a long time, possibly since the 70’s and all those Vietnam protest movies: the good guys. Amazon thought it could silence the protest voices by dropping Artificial . Instead it just sidelined itself. And now Neon (which picked up Artificial ), Sony ( The Social Reckoning ), HBO ( Musk ) and A24 ( You Can See Everything ) are all out there proudly putting the tech industry in check. Not for nothing do these four studios also have some of the smallest Silicon Valley involvement. (Though an A24 making deals with Google DeepMind, a Sony that produces hardware and an HBO now bankrolled by Larry Ellison shows how such entanglements also aren’t easily escapable in 2026.) AI will generate plenty of memeslop and cost-cutting; anyone who comes out of these movies thinking the great automation battle has been won in Hollywood, let alone the world, is either naive or self-deceiving. But it would be equally misguided to emerge into the daylight and think the films won’t matter at all, that a strong injection of anti-oligarchal humanity won’t course through the collective blood or change social views — that a long-term grudge, really, won’t be settled in some very productive ways. That grudge quote, by the way, comes from Elon Musk, who (ironic contrasts with his own lawsuit-happy pedigree aside ) now has been grudgily victimized himself — and by the very truth-seekers and storytellers he thought he’d dispatched when he bought Twitter. Talk about a good solve. title: Timothy Busfield Child Sex Abuse Case Dismissed Over Prosecutorial Misconduct
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All October 16, 2026 4:09pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Timothy Busfield Steven Ferdman/Getty Images The child sexual abuse case against Timothy Busfield has been tossed out by the judge overseeing the proceedings as he accused prosecutors of misconduct and violating grand jury statutes as the case began to move through the justice system. The charges of sexual assault involving two minors that were filed earlier this year in New Mexico against Busfield stem from time on the set of the TV series The Cleaning Lady , episodes of which he directed, between 2022 and 2024. The 69-year-old thirtysomething and Field of Dreams star, who went on to a prolific career as a director on television shows, is accused of sexually assaulting twin boys who appeared in several seasons of the show. Related Stories Movies Anna Paquin and Melissa Gilbert Call for Protection of Child Actors After Hayden Panettiere's Death: "Where Is the Collective Outrage?" TV Melissa Gilbert Believes Husband Timothy Busfield Will Be Exonerated of Child Sexual Abuse Charges Throughout his career as an actor and director, Busfield has faced multiple accusations from women of on-set groping and sexual assault; the outcomes of these accusations have varied from out-of-court settlements to dismissal of charges against him. He has been married to actor Melissa Gilbert since 2013. The 2026 accusations stem from a call placed to police in Albuquerque by a University of New Mexico physician who examined the boys and alerted them to allegations of abuse. After police had a difficult time finding him, a media frenzy followed and the actor was eventually arrested after he surrendered himself. The Bernalillo County District Attorney’s Office in New Mexico charged Busfield with four counts of criminal sexual contact of a child and he was released under his own recognizance ahead of the trial. An attorney for the actor has said that the charges are bogus and that the accusations come from the parents of the children who were looking for vengeance against Busfield for recasting the boys in the fourth season of the Fox series after they aged out of their roles. An investigation by Warner Bros. into the incident produced no evidence, and Busfield has passed a polygraph test regarding the allegations, his attorneys have told the court. But on Friday, it was the actions of prosecutors earlier this year during the grand jury process that sank the case — for now, at least. Judge Joseph Montano of the Second Judicial District Court of New Mexico in Albuquerque said prosecutors “failed to act in a fair and impartial manner” — but he did not close the door on future charges, leaving Busfield exposed to further legal action from New Mexico prosecutors. In his dismissal of the case, Judge Montano said that the state didn’t call certain witnesses after the grand jury asked to hear from them and failed to properly instruct jurors on procedures. In his conclusion, the judge lambasted prosecutors for failing to “act in a fair and impartial manner” and for violating grand jury statutes that are “designed to protect the structural integrity of our grand jury system.” The Hollywood Reporter reached out to the New Mexico Office of the Second Judicial District Attorney on Friday to discuss the grand jury proceedings and ask about plans for re-filing the case against Busfield, but did not immediately hear back. The New York Times reported that prosecutors are undecided as of Friday afternoon about refiling the charges. Nancy Laflin, a spokeswoman for the Second Judicial District Attorney’s Office of New Mexico, said in a statement sent to the outlet on Friday that her office “is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed.” Since the accusations against Busfield went public, he was dropped by talent agency Innovative Artists. title: John Amos’ Daughter Sues Brother for Wrongful Death Over Actor’s Death
full_text: Skip to main content By Winston Cho Plus Icon Winston Cho View All October 16, 2026 4:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source John Amos Brent Lewis/The Denver Post via Getty Images Logo text John Amos ‘ daughter is suing her brother and people in his orbit over the death of their father for elder abuse and wrongful death. The daughter, Shannon Amos, faults her brother, Kelly Christopher Amos, for delaying medical care while isolating the actor from his family and friends in the years leading up to his death. The lawsuit seeks a court order that, if granted, would bar K.C. Amos from inheriting from John Amos’ estate and to void the current will, plus unspecified damages. John Amos, 84, died in 2024 of natural causes. For years, his children have been engaged in an acrimonious battle over the actor’s care and finances. The lawsuit chronicles the last years of John Amos’ life. Around 2019, K.C. Amos started to keep his father from family and friends by shuffling him around various locations while monitoring his communications, manipulating the actor into believing that his family and friends were trying to exploit him, according to the complaint. For a three month period in 2023, all attempts by John Amos’ family to contact the actor were blocked, the lawsuit says. They were told to reach out to K.C. Amos. On multiple occasions, John Amos was left alone in unsafe and unsanitary conditions, including in hotels filled with trash, drug paraphernalia and soiled diapers, according to the complaint. Around this time, he was treated for an infection in his feet caused by maggots — one of numerous hospitalizations, prompting a call from Adult Protective Services over his care, the filing says. In an email to Shannon Amos, Elizabeth Bowling, a caregiver for John Amos, wrote of the actor’s living conditions, “The smell was horrid. There were no clean dishes. Mold had began to grow in the sink. Garbage bags/garbage laying where it was left. Food was left out on the counters and on the stove dried up. Counters and tables covered with gunk and what looked like marijuana and empty beer and liquor bottles around. No fresh food in the fridge.” During this period, the lawsuit says, John Amos missed treatments for prostate cancer and other health issues while continuing to do Cameo and low budget commercial appearances at the direction of his son. The matter was later referred to adult protective services in Colorado, the lawsuit claims, though John Amos was subsequently moved to Tennessee, where K.C. Amos struck a movie deal for his father. In August 2024, John Amos started to exhibit “obvious signs of a serious medical emergency,” the lawsuit claims. Despite this, Shannon Amos says her father’s his caregivers neglected to seek treatment for 13 hours. The actor was later brought to a hospital in Inglewood, where he died four hours after arriving. Shannon Amos accuses her brother of hiding their father’s death, which she discovered in October when it was reported in the media. The passing was announced by K.C. Amos, who allegedly had his father cremated without telling family members, according to the complaint. After John Amos’ death, K.C. Amos allegedly transferred substantial funds from his father to his personal bank accounts, the filing says. He later filed instated himself as sold owner of his father’s production outfit, Step and One Half Productions, securing control over the actor’s name and business interests, Shannon Amos claims. He also obtained exclusive access to John Amos’ roughly $6,300 SAG-AFTRA monthly pension and residuals while cutting the rest of the family out. The lawsuit challenges the current will. It claims that John Amos was tricked into signing documents that benefited K.C. Amos at the expense of other family members. A previous version of the will executed in 2020 accounted for beneficiaries that K.C. Amos didn’t think was appropriate, according to the complaint, which notes that the document “disappeared” days after it was signed. Another will was executed a year later that gave K.C. Amos power of attorney. In addition to K.C. Amos, the lawsuit names Belinda Foster, secretary for Step and One Half Productions, plus three companies formed by K.C. Amost. Two of them list Foster as a principal. One was formed in Colorado, weeks after law enforcement requested John Amos’ bank records. The other two were formed in California, roughly two months before the actor died. Shannon Amos alleges they were used to take over her father’s business interests. The legal action was filed in August in California state court. A petition had been filed in probate court asking for an emergency court order to freeze John Amos’ estate. The legal action was later withdrawn. THR

title: Austin Abrams Still Won’t Admit Which Was Tougher to Shoot, ‘Whalefall’ or ‘Resident Evil’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Brian Davids Plus Icon Brian Davids Writer PickYourBrian Follow Sign Up View All October 16, 2026 3:48pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for 20th Century Fox Logo text The autumn of Austin Abrams marches on with Whalefall , his second one-man genre exercise in the span of a month. The belle of the fall’s emotional survival tale joins Resident Evil in theaters as the latter continues to build on its $324 million worldwide box office gross. In Whalefall , co-written and directed by Brian Duffield , Abrams plays college student Jay Gardiner, who reluctantly returns home to California’s Central Coast a year after his estranged father, Mitt (Josh Brolin), responds to his terminal mesothelioma diagnosis by taking his own life at sea. Related Stories Movies Josh Brolin Talks the Personal Side of 'Whalefall' and the "Undeniable" Script for 'Sicario 3' Movies 'Street Fighter' Socks Away $4M in Previews as 'You Can See Everything' Takes $1.7M In a decision partly influenced by his mother (Elisabeth Shue) and two sisters (Jane Levy and Emily Rudd) having to visit an empty grave, Jay sets out to find his father’s remains on the ocean floor near Monastery Beach. The underlying hope is that the gesture will help him resolve their lingering differences stemming from his overly strict seafaring upbringing. But the plan goes belly-up almost immediately when a sperm whale pursuing a squid also swallows Jay, ensnaring him in its multichambered stomach. Like Resident Evil , Whalefall gives its protagonist just an hour to accomplish his goal, which in this case means escaping the whale’s innards before his oxygen tank runs dry. When The Hollywood Reporter last caught up with Abrams for Resident Evil , he refused to declare which film ended up being the more backbreaking ordeal. He certainly didn’t complain about splitting his head open during an elevator leap in Resident Evil ‘s third act or act fazed by nearly being crushed to death by a 150-pound blood bag in act two. But now that I’ve seen Whalefall , it seems that the only thing worse than actually being inside a whale’s stomach is pretending to be inside one. Yet Abrams still won’t kvetch about being crammed into a tiny whale-stomach set with a camera crew, while a half-dozen crew members surrounding the practical gut, wielding a gimbal, tossed him around like a wet rag doll. Duffield — who is also collaborating with Resident Evil filmmaker Zach Cregger on the upcoming Siren Head — believes his film takes the prize for putting their shared leading man through the wringer, given that his extremities weren’t restricted in Resident Evil . Abrams, meanwhile, continues to straddle the fence in gentlemanly fashion. “[The ability to move my limbs] was the nice part about Resident Evil . But they both have their perks and [pitfalls],” he tells THR in support of Whalefall ’s Oct. 16 theatrical release. To prepare for a scuba diver’s worst nightmare, Abrams earned the necessary certifications. He also visited a sperm whale sanctuary on a Caribbean island. Although the trip didn’t guarantee any face time with the wild animals, Abrams lucked out when they emerged for him, something they hadn’t done in the previous nine days. “It was beautiful. It was peaceful. It was the opposite of what you think it would be. You immediately know and feel how gentle and loving they are,” Abrams recalls. He also walked around his neighborhood in full scuba attire just to get used to the extra weight. While his neighbors weren’t alarmed enough by the unusual sight to call security, Abrams wasn’t as lucky during filming at Radford Studios in Studio City. “There’s a point where Jay gets visibly more distressed and blown-up looking,” Abrams shares. “I remember walking around the lot during that time and having security called on me just because I looked so fucked up.” Abrams, who generally avoids sharing too much about himself on a personal level, does reveal that his family is a little irked by how often his characters die in movies, a pattern that began with his first film, 2011’s Ticking Clock . A couple of years later, in his major studio debut, Abrams worked alongside Ryan Gosling in Gangster Squad until his shoeshine boy character caught a bullet during a mob ambush near a newsstand. (Brolin also stars in the 2013 crime pic, but didn’t share the screen with his future Weapons and Whalefall co-star.) Unintentionally, Abrams took a page out of Gosling’s playbook while preparing for his consecutive shoots on Whalefall and Resident Evil in 2025. Ahead of filming Peter Jackson’s The Lovely Bones in 2007, Gosling arrived to set with a beard and 60 extra pounds. Only 26 at the time, Gosling felt he needed to sell the appearance of a grieving father to two teenagers and a 4-year-old. Jackson was so thrown by Gosling’s unexpected character decisions that he recast him with Mark Wahlberg. Post- Whalefall , with little time to prepare for Resident Evil ‘s shoot in Prague, Abrams also adopted the “it’s easier to ask forgiveness than to get permission” approach to his own unannounced weight gain. He wanted his medical courier, Bryan, to look ill-equipped to handle a zombie outbreak, and seeking approval beforehand might’ve led financiers and producers, who typically want the most physically appealing lead actor possible, to discourage the idea. (Even Keanu Reeves’ beard nearly cost John Wick its financing.) Luckily, Cregger loved Abrams’ surprise choice. “I wanted Bryan to be a dude you look at and think he won’t be able to get out of this,” Abrams says. “I just had a strong impulse that I needed to do it. If you say you want to look a little bit different, it’s hard for people to imagine it. So it just felt like something that needed to be done, and I just went with it.” Below, during a conversation with THR , Abrams also discusses the careful handling of a particular letter in Whalefall . *** Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner in Brian Duffield ‘s Whalefall . 20th Century Studios I previously asked you which movie made you suffer more, and you chose to be Switzerland about it. But now that I’ve seen Whalefall , there’s no question it was more unbearable than Resident Evil . Are you willing to cop to it now? ( Laughs .) No, man. You said it, not me. Your Whalefall director, Brian Duffield , wasn’t proud of it, but he immediately took credit for his movie being the more punishing of the two. He did? He said, “The fact that Austin can move his arms and legs freely in Resident Evil gives Whalefall the edge.” That was the nice part about Resident Evil . But they both have their perks and [pitfalls]. I’m curious about your family’s response to these two new movies. Has it been hard for them to watch their baby boy in such precarious situations? I don’t know. I imagine to some degree it could be, but I also feel like everyone takes it okay. I feel like they’d prefer if I died less in some of them, but other than that, I think they do alright. Yeah, that has been a pattern in your work. The Line was especially brutal. Yeah, man. It’s been that way from the beginning. I don’t know why. It’s funny you say that because I’m about to reference the first major one. Go ahead! (L-r) Director Brian Duffield and Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner on the set of Whalefall . Jennifer Clasen/20th Century Studios Well, the first thing that struck me about Whalefall was how different you looked as Jay, especially since you shot it right before Resident Evil . Then I read that you gained weight for Bryan in Resident Evil . Given how little time you had in between, did you microwave tubs of Häagen-Dazs once you got to Prague and gorge yourself? ( Laughs .) Oh man. Yeah, you just do whatever you can. I wanted Bryan to be a dude you look at and think he won’t be able to get out of this. I didn’t want him to look like someone who runs laps in his free time or something like that. So it was a close period of time, but there wasn’t really any science to it. You just do whatever you can to get where you need to go. The Häagen-Dazs method? I don’t know. Just pure ice cream is preferable. It was a bold move not to tell Zach Cregger you were packing on some pounds. There’s a famous story involving your shoe-shine customer, Ryan Gosling. [ In Gangster Squad , Gosling’s character urged Abrams’ young shoeshiner to go home, but he didn’t listen and fell victim to mob-related gunfire. ] ( Laughs .) Shoe-shine customer, that’s funny. He showed up on a Peter Jackson set 60 pounds heavier from drinking melted Häagen-Dazs, only he didn’t tell Jackson he was doing it. So that’s the reason why Mark Wahlberg is now the one who starred in The Lovely Bones . Yeah, but I just had a strong impulse that I needed to do it. So I just went from there. If you say you want to look a little bit different, it’s hard for people to imagine it. So it just felt like something that needed to be done, and I just went with it. Most importantly, Zach loved the choice. I hope so. He said so. ( Laughs. ) Yeah. By all accounts, you were a great sport when filming inside each whale stomach, but was there a day where you needed to be let out early because it was just too much? I don’t know if we had that situation. The nature of the movie meant welcoming whatever difficulty came with it. When something is welcomed, it makes it less difficult. You don’t want to get out of any difficulty. You want to keep it there [for the sake of the scene]. Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner in Brian Duffield’s Whalefall . 20th Century Studios I read that you walked around your neighborhood in scuba gear to get used to the weight. Did your neighbors give you any weird looks or call the police about some guy loitering in scuba apparatus? I can’t remember if there were any funny looks or not. This is a little different from what you’re talking about, but there’s a point where Jay gets visibly more distressed and blown-up looking. I remember walking around the lot during that time and having security called on me just because I looked so fucked up. Before filming, you traveled to a Caribbean island to get in the water with some real sperm whales, and they appeared for you, something they don’t always do for people. Were you trembling with fear? Or was it more peaceful than it sounds? Man, it was beautiful. It was peaceful. It was the opposite of what you think it would be. You immediately know and feel how gentle and loving they are. Also, if they’re not interested in you, they’ll just dive back down. They can very easily avoid you if they want to, at least in this circumstance. But it was just an immensely moving experience, and I’m super grateful. You don’t know if any whales are going to be around, and you also don’t know if they’re going to have any interest in hanging out for a little bit. So I got really, really lucky with that. You and Josh Brolin knew each other from Weapons , but given how intense Jay and Mitt’s scenes are, did you avoid socializing before the scene work? [ Brolin was also in Gangster Squad , but he and Abrams didn’t share the screen .] Thankfully, there was already a level of love and trust from knowing one another beforehand. When it comes to the work and their relationship, there’s a certain point where it’s not necessarily helpful to be palling around together. Sometimes it’s important and useful to strip that stuff away, and sometimes it’s not. It’s whatever feels the most useful, and hopefully it is. But yeah, there was certainly less [socializing] than there’d normally be. It’s always different when you’re working and doing whatever you need to do to lend a feeling to the scene. So that’s my answer or non-answer to that. (L-R): Austin Abrams as Jay Gardiner and Josh Brolin as Mitt Gardiner in Brian Duffield’s Whalefall . 20th Century Studios There was an early cut of the movie where Mitt’s letter to Jay was at least partially visible, but then the studio urged Brian to remove any glimpse. Are you ever going to reveal what Jay’s letter said? Unh-unh. Good. Keep that secret for the rest of your life. Yeah. Maybe I’ll tell people personally. That’s cool, but don’t tell people like me. We don’t deserve it. ( Laughs .) It’s richer this way. I really feel that way. If you put your own interpretation on it, that’s potentially going to be more meaningful and interesting than whatever was written. You’re also projecting whatever you wish a family member had said to you if they’d written you a letter before they died. That’s valuable. So there’s value in the not knowing. Austin Abrams as Bryan in Zach Cregger ‘s Resident Evil . Dušan Martinček/Sony Pictures Can we speed-round some Resident follow-ups in our waning moments? Oh boy. Whatcha got for me? The internet believes the Sundress Woman was actually the farmer’s wife. That would explain why she was relatively close to the farm in the first place. Do you believe that to be true? That’s shown in there. You must be referring to the photo of the farmer and his wife. I looked up the actor (Andrea Miltnerová) who plays the Sundress Woman, and compared her with the woman in that photo. While I’m 99.9 percent certain it’s the same person, I hesitate to call that confirmation. All I’m saying is that it’s in there. I read a draft of the script, and in the second phone call with Michelle (then known as Ashley) in the car, Bryan eventually tells her straight up that he wants to have a kid with her, only she couldn’t hear him because of bad cell service. Did you ever shoot that version? Unh-unh. No. The Paul Walter Hauser character, Paul, used to be a woman named Pauline, and she went with Bryan to the rat sewer before getting consumed by them. Bryan then mowed down her rat-infested body. Do you know why Zach dropped any version of that? I don’t know what you read. It must have been a very early draft. Yeah, you found an early one. The dog also bit Bryan first and caused his infection, not the little girl. Yeah, yeah, yeah. There’s certain parts of these that I’m remembering, but the one with Pauline and the rats, I don’t remember that. The syringe originally broke inside the lab, but Zach happened to shoot another version with it outside in case he changed his mind in post. Did he let you find out about that switch when you watched it for the first time? We talked about that. That was something we’d been talking about. *** Whalefall is now paying in movie theaters nationwide . THR

title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Directing Duo Los Javis Reveal How Spanish Sensation Became “The Journey Of Our Lives”
full_text: Skip to main content By Baz Bamigboye Baz Bamigboye Columnist/International Editor At Large @BazBam More Stories By Baz Sacha Baron Cohen Confirmed To Star In Quentin Tarantino’s ‘The Popinjay Cavalier’ West End Stage Play With Dates & On Sale Window Announced Breaking Baz: Why LFF Opener ‘Elsinore’ Is A Triumphant Epitaph For An Extraordinary Man Breaking Baz: Anthony Mackie Returning To Broadway To Play Macbeth After 16-Year Absence From The Stage View All October 16, 2026 3:15pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Penelope Cruz in ‘La Bola Negra’ Carla Oset/Netflix Penélope Cruz had been a muse to Los Javis — the moniker for Spanish filmmakers Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo — for years before they met for lunch to persuade her to play a singer (more a force of nature, really) in La Bola Negra , an electrifying sensation at Cannes that’s now Spain’s entry for best international feature film Oscar . “I saw her in a clip of Jamón Jamón ,” says Ambrossi, referring to Bigas Luna’s 1992 picture, in which Cruz appeared for the first time opposite her now-husband Javier Bardem. “I was young, and I thought, ‘Who is she ?!’ ” Related Stories Reviews ‘La Bola Negra’ Review: Spain’s Javier Calvo And Javier Ambrossi Capture Hearts With Their Unashamedly Romantic Decades-Spanning Drama – Cannes Film Festival Festivals Penélope Cruz’s ‘La Bola Negra’ Lands 20-Minute Ovation From Overjoyed Audience At Cannes Calvo was similarly enchanted when he saw Cruz in Pedro Almodóvar’s 1999 Oscar winner All About My Mother . “She’s got that material of the stars,” he says. “When you put a camera in front of her, she can do anything, and she doesn’t even realize what she’s doing. There’s a power , there’s a force guiding her, and that’s amazing to see first-hand.” Watch on Deadline Los Javis wanted Cruz for a small but pivotal role in their epic tale La Bola Negra , the intertwined story of three gay men who exist in three different time periods in Spain. In 1932, Carlos (Milo Quifes) is a young man in Grenada at a time when Spain is lurching uncomfortably towards an ever-increasing spiteful intolerance of homosexuality. In 1937, against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War, Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) and Rafael ( Miguel Bernardeau ) are soldiers from opposing political divides brought closer by the conflict. And in 2017, Alberto (Carlos González) is a playwright from Madrid who engages with an eminent Federico Garcia Lorca scholar (played by another Hollywood star, Glenn Close , speaking fluent Spanish) in a storyline that links the characters in the prior timelines.

title: ‘Crystal Lake’s Gwendolyn Sundstrom On Grace’s Friendship With Jason, “Learning A Lot” From Linda Cardellini & That Killer Twist
full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘9-1-1: Nashville’ Pays Tribute To Chad Lowe’s Daughter Fiona With Title Card In Season 2 Premiere KJ Apa Asked ‘Riverdale’ Showrunner Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa For ‘Afterlife with Archie’ Cameo: “I Don’t Know Who I’d Play” Brad Caleb Kane Teases ‘It: Welcome to Derry’ Is “Bigger” In Season 2 With “A Different Kind Of Pennywise” View All October 16, 2026 3:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Gwendolyn Sundstrom as Grace in 'Crystal Lake' Peacock SPOILER ALERT: This post contains details about Peacock ‘s series Crystal Lake . While Crystal Lake revisits several familiar locals from the Friday the 13th franchise, Gwendolyn Sundstrom brings a fresh role to the slasher prequel series. Now available to stream on Peacock, Sundstrom told Deadline that Jason Voorhees’ (Callum Vinson) childhood friend Grace has been her “favorite character so far” to play, filming the Brad Caleb Kane series in New Jersey when she was only 13. Related Stories News ‘Crystal Lake’s Linda Cardellini Used Pam Voorhees’ Grief As “Fuel For Her Rage,” Reveals Her Favorite Kill Scenes: “Feels A Little Too Good” News Brad Caleb Kane On Making ‘Crystal Lake’ A “Small-Town Show” In Same N.J. Locations Where ‘Friday The 13th’ Filmed, “Faithfully” Re-Creating An Iconic Scene & “Twin Peaks-y” Plans For Season 2 “It was fun, ’cause in real life I don’t really relate to Grace that much, but it was fun to try and find things from my life that I could put into Grace and really play her,” explained Sundstrom. “But I had a great day every day on set, it was amazing.” Watch on Deadline As the series recounts the accidental drowning of young Jason that was first mentioned in the original 1980 movie, the opening scene of the first episode reveals Grace throwing a bully’s ball out into the lake after he was teasing Jason. While counselors Claudette (Danielle Kotch) and Barry (Phoenix Parnevik) sneak off to hook up, Jason goes after the ball, only to drown in the depths of Crystal Lake. Jason and Grace’s endearing adolescent friendship continues to play out through flashbacks as she struggles to mourn his death amid the usual complications of growing up. “I think it was really helpful that Callum and I had really good chemistry in real life too, but I think building Grace as a character, she’s also kind of an underdog,” explained Sundstrom. “She also doesn’t have very many friends, so I think we could kind of work off each other and portray that kind of character cause we’re so similar.” With nowhere to put her maternal love after the loss of her son Jason, Pam Voorhees ( Linda Cardellini ) soon takes an interest in Grace, whose own mom appears to be abusive and neglectful. “I loved working with Linda. She was so nice,” Sundstrom said. “I definitely learned a lot from her. I think when Pam takes on kind of this maternal role, I think that’s something Grace, first of all, isn’t really used to, and also doesn’t really want. I think she’s trying to push Pam away, and Pam only wants to get even closer and even more protective, and I think that’s kind of a conflict that the two characters have.” After finding a new “family” in a pack of traveling hippies, Grace ends up on a drug trip that results in a deconstruction of the very first kill in the Friday the 13th franchise. But instead of Pam, it’s revealed that Grace was the person to kill Claudette and Barry in that first-person POV sequence. Callum Vinson as Jason Voorhees and Gwendolyn Sundstrom as Grace in ‘Crystal Lake’ “I had a lot of fun with that scene,” said Sundstrom. “I definitely like filming more dramatic, gritty, emotional things, so that was really fun for me.” And while diehard fans of the franchise might not be down with the retcon of such an iconic kill scene, Kane explained he wanted to “blow people’s minds” and “give the audience something different to chew on.” “You have to re-contextualize it, and you want a shock,” explained Kane. “We come to these movies for the rollercoaster ride of it, we come to these movies for the jaw-drop of it. If you think you know everything from the movie coming into the TV series, and then we just go, ‘yeah, it’s exactly as you thought it was,’ that’s no fun.” Linda Cardellini as Pam Voorhees and Gwendolyn Sundstrom as Grace in ‘Crystal Lake’ Now streaming on Peacock, Crystal Lake stars Cardellini as Pam Voorhees, who struggles to grieve after her son Jason drowned the summer before. title: ‘Street Fighter’ Socking $30M, ‘You Can See Everything’ Beaming 2nd Best Opening For Documentary At $12M – Friday Box Office Update
full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony ‘Street Fighter’ Socking $30M, ‘You Can See Everything’ Beaming 2nd Best Opening For Documentary At $12M – Friday Box Office Update Chase Infiniti-Starring ‘The Julia Set’ Acquired By Sony Pictures Classics After TIFF Premiere Indie Film Studio Bleecker Street Bought By Outerlight Entertainment View All October 16, 2026 2:39pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji in 'Street Fighter' Paramount FRIDAY PM UPDATE: Street Fighter is currently coming in at the lower end of expectations with a $30M opening after a $12.5M Friday (including previews) at 3,575 theaters, which includes previews. Hopefully Saturday can keep it together with family traffic. Note, the only MLB playoff game this weekend is between Tampa Bay and the Cleveland Guardians, so don’t expect a slowdown at the box office. Related Stories News ‘Street Fighter’ Review: Cheesy, Action-Packed Movie Reboot Has A Game Cast That Should Please Fans Looking To Relive The ’90s Reviews ‘You Can See Everything’ Review: Shocking Elizabeth Holmes Documentary With Nathan Fielder Is Like No Other You Have Ever Seen – Telluride Film Festival Interesting to note that the opening here alone is close to what the original 1994 take on the Capcom game finaled at which was $33.4M (unadjusted for inflation). That pic starred Jean-Claude Van Damme and opened to $6.8M via Universal. The first Legendary title under its new deal with Paramount had a big social media universe grab heading into the weekend with 920.6M from TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and X. That’s bigger than other videogame movies, Legendary’s Minecraft Movie (772.4M), Mortal Kombat 2 (452.6M) and Five Nights at Freddy ‘s (488.5M). This is all according to RelishMix. One of the big early September pushes for Street Fighter was a novel playable “The Street Fighter Combo Trailer” which launched on YouTube Playables, which placed film footage inside a virtual arcade cabinet and utilized game-style mechanics. Watch on Deadline The Rotten Tomatoes audience score for Street Fighter is currently at 80%, not far from the 86% of Mortal Kombat 2, which was rated-R, but based on a similar martial arts video game born during the Gen X era. A24’s You Can See Everything with a 99% RT audience score and an expected opening around $12M after a $5.3M Friday (including previews) at 885 theaters is bound to unseat Melania which debuted to $7.1M and was called the best opening for a documentary in ten years. The intel we have shows that You Can See Everything is the second best opening for a documentary in the past 17 years (not counting concert films), behind 2004’s Fahrenheit 9/11 ($23.9M) and ahead of Disney’s 2012 Chimpanzee at $10.6M. The Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim-directed trippy non-fiction film follows Theranos architect Elizabeth Holmes and her partner Billy Evans in the run-up to the former’s stay in a federal prison. Universal Blumhouse Atomic Monster’s Other Mommy at 3,370 theaters is posting a second Friday of $2.4M and second weekend of $7.4M in third, -73%, for a running cume of $43.9M . That drop after last weekend’s D+ CinemaScore is to be expected. Getting beached is 20th Century Studio’s Whalefall with a $2.6M Friday (including previews) and $6M-$7M opening, far below the $11M that tracking was spotting. Many enjoy watching Austin Abrams getting swallowed by zombies, Zach Cregger style. No one wants to watch him go through a Pinocchio experience, meaning being eaten by a whale. The audience score is 82% on RT. Focus Features’ Sense & Sensibility at 2,545 sites is seeing a Friday of $3M, and 3-day of $6M . That result is just $600K shy of the $6.6M that Focus’ Conclave opened to, but that was in fewer theaters, that being 1,753. No RT audience score yet. The previous 1995 Ang Lee-directed take of the Jane Austen classic was a platform release back in the day, but legged its way to a $43.4M domestic final. UPDATE after exclusive: Paramount/Legendary/Capcom’s Street Fighter rang up exactly what we saw last night, $4 million in previews , while A24’s zany Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything filed $1.75M , but with awesome exits (e.g., 92% definite recommend, 100% positive score). 20th Century Studios’ Whalefall was at $900,000 from Thursday’s showtimes, while Focus Features’ Sense & Sensibility revival in all previews (not just last night) did $1.15M . You Can See Everything drew 50-50 male-female while the Gen-Z’ers came out in bulk at 75% under 35 in Los Angeles and New York last night. Letterboxd is now up to 4.7 and ranking among the top 50 movies of all time. Whalefall, which was shot in California for a net $60M, follows Jay Gardiner (Austin Abrams), who after the death of his father (Josh Brolin) goes diving off the central coast in search of his remains and is swallowed by a massive sperm whale. While trapped inside its belly with only one hour of oxygen left, Jay comes to realize that the hard-earned lessons his father imparted may be the key to his escape. The thriller is booked at 3,065 theatres including 500 Premium Large Format screens and 250 D-Box/Motion screens. Last night’s previews are far below the $2M made by the recent fall thriller Heart of the Beast, which went on to open to $20M (granted, that one starred Brad Pitt). The Los Angeles Dodgers aren’t going to the World Series again this year as the Milwaukee Brewers swept them out of the National League Championship Series last night. Tampa Bay and Cleveland are still duking it out in the ALCS with games tonight and Saturday. Translation: This year’s World Series won’t have any impact on box office capitals New York City and L.A. Below is this week’s top 5: 1.) Other Mommy (Uni) 3,365 theaters, Wk $36.5M /Wk 1 2.) Verity (AMZ) 3,572 theaters, Wk $17.5M (-59%), Total $59.9M /Wk 2 3.) Resident Evil (Sony) 3,085 theaters, Wk $12.8M (-28%), Total $142.9M /Wk 4 4.) Heart of the Beast (Par) 3,365 theaters, Wk $10.9M (-28%), Total $53.4M /Wk 3 5.) Forgotten Island (Uni) 2,898 theaters, Wk $7.09M (-24%), Total $32.8M /Wk 3 PREVIOUSLY, Thursday EXCLUSIVE: Paramount/Legendary’s PG-13 take of the Capcom video game Street Fighter is off to a solid start Thursday night with around $4 million after showtimes that began at 2 p.m. (further boosted by a 7 p.m. fan showtime). The expectation is for the fisticuffs feature to open north of $30M; the pic cost a net $82M co-financed by Legendary and Capcom. Per sources, Street Figther ‘s preview estimate is under the $5.2M Thursday made by New Line’s R-rated Mortal Kombat 2 , based on the Midway video game and which bowed in mid-May. One of the main differences between the two martial arts video games is that Street Fighter debuted in 1987, while Mortal Kombat followed in pizza parlors and arcades in 1992. Mortal Kombat 2 earlier this year had previews that began at 3 p.m. with a first Friday of $16.8M and 3-day of $38.5M. There’s a mid-fall break going on now, which will hopefully trigger traffic to Street Fighter ; Rentrak reports 21% K-12 schools off and 7% colleges. Street Fighter ‘s previews are also ahead of Paramount’s 2020 pre-Covid Sonic the Hedgehog at $3M, leading to a first Friday of $20.9M and 3-day of $58M. However, that pic played over the Presidents Day holiday frame and was rated PG. Critics bruised Street Fighter with 47% on Rotten Tomatoes. Impressive for the anomaly that it is out of the gate, the three-hour documentary You Can See Everything from A24 is filing around $2M in previews that began at 3 p.m. By comparison, the last documentary to post the decade’s best start at the domestic box office, Amazon MGM Studios’ Melania, bowed to $7.1M sans previews. Lance Oppenheim co-directed You Can See Everything with the doc’s host Nathan Fielder, who follows fallen Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes before her stint in federal prison. Oppenheim’s previous movie, also his first narrative feature, this fall’s Primetime, posted previews of $2.7M; those began at 4 p.m. and turned into an $18.8M opening. Conservative estimates heading into this weekend had You Can See Everything in the high single-digit range, but confidence is growing that this critically acclaimed (100% fresh RT and 98% RT audience score) movie can open to north of $10M, which would outstrip Melania ‘s previous opening domestic record for a documentary. You Can See Everything was shot over four years and cost less than $10M, with a marketing budget that was also under $10M.
